projects.name: Encore
projects.description: Daily grid logic puzzles with infinite practice, curated catalogues, and replay-any-day seeds.

caseStudy.claim: Daily grid logic puzzles (Stitch, Quilt, Weave) with deterministic seeds on a Cloudflare Worker + Neon stack.
caseStudy.role: Sole engineer — puzzle engine, API, web client, and deploy

metrics.label: puzzle families live (Stitch, Quilt, Weave)
Worker serving both the SPA and /v1 API

caseStudy.problem: Most daily games hide their generators; players cannot trust practice boards or replay a past day fairly. Encore needed a deterministic engine and one Worker for SPA + API.

sections.title: Deterministic puzzle engine
sections.body:
Players land on the current day’s board with practice, catalogue, and archive modes one tap away.

The same (seed, version) pair yields identical boards in every mode, so a practice run is the same puzzle someone else replays from the archive.
sections.imageAlt: Encore home screen showing the daily grid puzzle and the Stitch, Quilt, and Weave modes

sections.title: Shared Cloudflare Worker
sections.body:
SPA and /v1 API share one Worker with Neon Postgres (FORCE RLS), Better Auth, and first-party analytics.

Keeps game surfaces and account sync on one deploy unit.
sections.imageAlt: Encore catalogue and progress surfaces below the fold on encore.casa

decisions.choice: Deterministic seeded generation
decisions.why: Fair daily + replayable practice without storing every board bitmap.
decisions.tradeoff: Engine versioning must stay explicit when generators change.

decisions.choice: Postgres FORCE RLS with CI proofs
decisions.why: Guest and account data must not leak across tenants.
decisions.tradeoff: More migration and policy discipline.

decisions.choice: No iframe embed of encore.casa
decisions.why: Production CSP uses frame-ancestors none.
decisions.tradeoff: Case study uses screenshot/CTA overlay instead of live embed.

caseStudy.outcome: Live at encore.casa with Stitch, Quilt, Weave (Lattice beta), catalogues, guest/account progress, soft leaderboards, and PWA install — Premium Stripe path wired but flagged off.

projects.name: Baseer Portfolio
projects.description: Marketing CV site for Baseer with a freeform visual CMS, first-party analytics, and sector case studies.

caseStudy.claim: Marketing CV site for Baseer with a freeform visual CMS, first-party analytics, and sector case studies.
caseStudy.role: Sole engineer — CMS, Worker API, analytics, and marketing surfaces

metrics.label: Worker hosting site, CMS, and analytics
third-party analytics scripts

caseStudy.problem:
A CV site is only useful if its owner can restyle it without a developer, and template builders lock content into fixed slots.

Baseer needed sector case studies he could rearrange freely, plus visitor insight without handing traffic data to a third-party tracker.

sections.title: Marketing site and sector case studies
sections.body:
A CV-led landing page with sector case studies, each editable as freeform content rather than a fixed template field.

Motion and layout are tuned for a marketing read rather than a document dump.
sections.imageAlt: Baseer portfolio landing page with headline and sector navigation

sections.title: Freeform CMS and first-party analytics
sections.body:
Better Auth gates a visual CMS that writes to Neon Postgres through Drizzle, with media on R2.

Analytics are collected by the same Worker, so visitor data never leaves the site’s own domain.
sections.imageAlt: Baseer portfolio case-study content section further down the page

decisions.choice: Freeform visual CMS over a fixed template
decisions.why: The owner edits layout and copy directly instead of filing change requests.
decisions.tradeoff: More validation and migration work than a fixed set of content fields.

decisions.choice: First-party analytics inside the same Worker
decisions.why: Keeps visitor data on the site’s own domain and avoids loading a third-party tracker.
decisions.tradeoff: Reporting, retention, and dashboards are ours to build and maintain.

decisions.choice: Neon Postgres with Drizzle behind Hono
decisions.why: Content and analytics share one typed relational schema with cheap edge reads.
decisions.tradeoff: Connection handling from Workers needs deliberate pooling.

caseStudy.outcome: Live at baseer.co.uk: marketing site, sector case studies, R2-backed media, a Better Auth-protected visual CMS, and first-party analytics on a single Cloudflare deploy.

projects.name: Docket
projects.description: Personal job-application tracker with Kanban, list, stats, docs, reminders, and email alerts—built for a single owner, no login.

caseStudy.claim: Personal job-application tracker with Kanban, list, stats, docs, reminders, and email alerts—built for a single owner, no login.
caseStudy.role: Sole engineer — product, API, and infrastructure
caseStudy.timeline: 2026 · in daily use, live at jobtracker.humza-butt.space

metrics.label: tracker surfaces: Kanban, list, stats, docs, reminders
login screens — single-owner by design

caseStudy.problem:
A spreadsheet of applications loses the timeline: which stage each role is at, which CV version was sent, and when a follow-up is due.

Docket has exactly one user, so accounts, tenancy, and onboarding would have been pure overhead on top of the tracking itself.

sections.title: Kanban and list tracking
sections.body:
Applications move across stages on a Kanban board, with a dense list view for bulk edits and search.

Both views read the same Neon Postgres records, so state never diverges between them.
sections.imageAlt: Docket job application Kanban board with applications grouped by stage

sections.title: Stats, documents, and reminders
sections.body:
Recharts dashboards summarise pipeline health, while CVs and cover letters live on R2 against each application.

Resend sends reminder emails so follow-up dates do not depend on remembering to open the app.
sections.imageAlt: Docket dashboard showing application statistics and document tools

decisions.choice: No login — single-owner access model
decisions.why: With one user, auth would add friction and attack surface without protecting anything extra.
decisions.tradeoff: Access control lives at the deployment edge rather than in application code.

decisions.choice: R2 for CV and cover-letter storage
decisions.why: Documents belong next to the application record, not in a folder on one laptop.
decisions.tradeoff: Object lifecycle and orphan cleanup become the app’s responsibility.

decisions.choice: Resend for reminder email
decisions.why: Deadline nudges have to land reliably without running a mail server.
decisions.tradeoff: An external dependency sits on the critical reminder path.

caseStudy.outcome: Live at jobtracker.humza-butt.space with Kanban and list tracking, Zod-validated writes, Recharts stats, R2 document storage, reminders, and Resend email alerts.

projects.name: Docket (Baseer)
projects.description: Baseer's job-application tracker with kanban, list tools, docs, stats, and Resend alerts—single owner, no login.

caseStudy.claim: Baseer's job-application tracker with kanban, list tools, docs, stats, and Resend alerts—single owner, no login.
caseStudy.role: Sole engineer — rebuilt Docket as a second single-owner instance

metrics.label: independent single-owner deploys from one codebase
shared user data between instances

caseStudy.problem:
Baseer wanted the same application tracking as Docket, but on his own domain, with his own data and branding.

Turning a single-owner tool into a multi-tenant product would have introduced accounts and permissions that neither owner asked for.

sections.title: Owner’s pipeline on its own domain
sections.body:
A dedicated deploy at docket.baseer.co.uk with Baseer’s branding, kanban stages, and list tools.

No sign-in, no tenant switcher — the instance belongs to one person.
sections.imageAlt: Docket (Baseer) application board on docket.baseer.co.uk

sections.title: Documents, stats, and alerts
sections.body:
R2 stores CVs and letters per application, Recharts renders pipeline stats, and Resend handles reminder mail.

Drizzle schemas are shared with the original Docket so features port cleanly between instances.
sections.imageAlt: Docket (Baseer) statistics and document management view

decisions.choice: A separate deploy per owner instead of multi-tenancy
decisions.why: Two single-owner instances keep data physically separated with no permission model to get wrong.
decisions.tradeoff: Feature work has to be ported between deploys rather than shipped once.

decisions.choice: Turborepo with shared packages
decisions.why: Keeps the two Docket surfaces from drifting apart as either one changes.
decisions.tradeoff: Monorepo tooling overhead on a deliberately small product.

decisions.choice: Cloudflare Pages and Workers over Neon
decisions.why: Static client, edge API, and durable Postgres with no servers to operate.
decisions.tradeoff: Edge database connections need pooling care under bursty use.

caseStudy.outcome: Live at docket.baseer.co.uk with kanban and list tools, R2 document storage, Recharts stats, and Resend alerts running on Baseer’s own domain and data.

projects.name: Buzzer
projects.description: LifeSmart’s teacher-led live financial literacy game for schools — anonymous pupil teams, front screen, real-time play.

caseStudy.claim: LifeSmart’s teacher-led live financial literacy game for schools — anonymous pupil teams, front screen, real-time play.
caseStudy.role: Full-stack engineer — realtime server, teacher console, and pupil client

metrics.label: synchronised surfaces: teacher, front screen, pupil
pupil accounts or personal data collected

caseStudy.problem:
Classroom quiz tools usually make every pupil sign in, which burns lesson time and creates pupil data a school then has to safeguard.

Buzzer had to keep a teacher console, a projected front screen, and a room full of pupil devices in lockstep using anonymous teams only.

sections.title: Anonymous team join and live play
sections.body:
Pupils join a room code as a team — no account, no email — while the teacher drives the round from their own console and the front screen projects state to the class.

Buzz order, scoring, and round transitions are resolved by the server so no device can win by having a faster clock.
sections.imageAlt: Buzzer join screen for LifeSmart’s classroom financial literacy game

decisions.choice: A Durable Object per game room
decisions.why: One object owns each room’s state, giving a single authority for buzz order and scores over WebSockets.
decisions.tradeoff: Room lifetime and hibernation have to be handled explicitly.

decisions.choice: Anonymous pupil teams
decisions.why: Schools avoid collecting pupil identities, and a team is in the game within seconds.
decisions.tradeoff: No cross-session pupil history to build progression on.

decisions.choice: Distinct teacher, front-screen, and pupil views
decisions.why: Each audience needs different information from the same underlying game state.
decisions.tradeoff: Three surfaces to keep correct on every state transition.

caseStudy.outcome: Live at buzzer.lifesmartfinance.com as LifeSmart’s teacher-led classroom game: anonymous team join, server-ordered buzz-in, projected front screen, and live scoring on Cloudflare Durable Objects.

projects.name: Oche
projects.description: Live venue scoreboard for competitive-socialising sessions: real-time scores, match history, and game video on Cloudflare.

caseStudy.claim: Live venue scoreboard for competitive-socialising sessions: real-time scores, match history, and game video on Cloudflare.
caseStudy.role: Sole engineer — realtime scoreboard, venue dashboard, and media pipeline

metrics.label: Durable Object owning each live venue session
surfaces: big screen, player device, venue dashboard

caseStudy.problem:
Competitive-socialising venues score sessions on paper or one person’s phone, so nobody else at the table can see the running state and nothing survives the night.

Oche needed a shared live scoreboard, durable match history, and clip playback a venue could run on a big screen.

sections.title: Live session scoreboard
sections.body:
Scores update over WebSockets from a Durable Object that owns the session, so every screen in the venue shows the same state without polling.

Built to be readable across a room, not just on a phone.
sections.imageAlt: Oche live venue scoreboard showing an in-progress session

sections.title: Match history and game video
sections.body:
Completed sessions are written to Neon Postgres so history outlives the room object, with game video stored on R2 and played back against each match.

Zod validates every write on the way in.
sections.imageAlt: Oche match history and session detail view

decisions.choice: Durable Objects and WebSockets per session
decisions.why: Everyone at the oche sees the same score at the same time without clients polling an API.
decisions.tradeoff: Session state must be flushed to Postgres to survive the object’s lifetime.

decisions.choice: R2 for game video
decisions.why: Clips live next to the match record and stream out without egress charges.
decisions.tradeoff: Media lifecycle and storage growth need active management.

decisions.choice: PWA install for venue screens
decisions.why: Venue tablets and TVs run it full-screen without going through an app store.
decisions.tradeoff: Offline and stale-cache behaviour has to be handled deliberately.

caseStudy.outcome: Live at oche.humza-butt.space with real-time session scoring on Durable Objects, match history persisted to Neon Postgres, game video on R2, and an installable PWA for venue screens.

projects.name: Blitz
projects.description: Chrome extension that AI-tailors your CV per job (BYOK), then fills applications on major ATS boards after you review.

caseStudy.claim: Chrome extension that AI-tailors your CV per job (BYOK), then fills applications on major ATS boards after you review.
caseStudy.role: Sole engineer — extension, ATS adapters, and BYOK key handling

metrics.label: users supply their own model API key
applications submitted without human review

caseStudy.problem:
Tailoring a CV to each posting is the slowest part of applying, but tools that auto-submit on your behalf are a liability you cannot undo.

Blitz had to do the rewriting and the form filling while leaving the final submit to the human — and without holding anyone’s model API key on a server.

sections.title: Tailor, review, then fill
sections.body:
The extension reads the posting, rewrites the CV against it with the user’s own model key, and shows the result for approval.

Only after review does it populate the application form on the job board.
sections.imageAlt: Blitz landing page explaining AI CV tailoring for job applications

sections.title: Supported boards and account surface
sections.body:
Per-board content scripts handle the field structures of the major ATS providers, with a Supabase-backed account and a Cloudflare Worker for the hosted pieces.

Vitest and Playwright cover the adapters, which are the parts most likely to break when a board changes.
sections.imageAlt: Blitz marketing site section covering supported job boards and workflow

decisions.choice: Bring-your-own-key for the AI model
decisions.why: Users keep control and cost of their own model usage, and no shared key sits on our infrastructure.
decisions.tradeoff: Onboarding asks for an API key before the user sees any value.

decisions.choice: A review gate before any form is filled
decisions.why: An automated submission to a real employer cannot be taken back.
decisions.tradeoff: Slower than tools that promise fully automatic applying.

decisions.choice: Per-board content-script adapters
decisions.why: Major ATS boards each expose different field names and DOM structures.
decisions.tradeoff: Adapters break whenever a board ships a redesign.

caseStudy.outcome: Shipped a Chrome extension that tailors a CV per posting using the user’s own key and fills applications on major ATS boards after review, with the marketing and account site live at blitzai.online.

projects.name: 501 Feature Cards
projects.description: Accessible, CMS-agnostic Web Component replacing hard-coded landing-page stat cards—vanilla JS, Shadow DOM, live editor demo.

caseStudy.claim: Accessible, CMS-agnostic Web Component replacing hard-coded landing-page stat cards—vanilla JS, Shadow DOM, live editor demo.
caseStudy.role: Sole engineer and maintainer of the open-source component

metrics.label: framework dependencies — vanilla Web Component
custom element tag to drop into any CMS

caseStudy.problem:
501’s landing-page stat cards were hard-coded, so every copy change needed a developer and a deploy.

The replacement had to work inside whatever CMS or framework a page already used, stay accessible, and be safe for non-developers to edit.

sections.title: Live editor demo
sections.body:
The demo site lets you edit card configuration and see the component re-render immediately, which is how non-developers verify content before publishing.

Deployed on Cloudflare Pages with a Worker for the demo endpoints.
sections.imageAlt: 501 Feature Cards demo page showing configurable stat cards

sections.title: Shadow DOM isolation and accessibility
sections.body:
Shadow DOM keeps host page styles from leaking in and component styles from leaking out, with theming exposed through explicit custom properties.

Zod validates configuration, and Vitest plus Playwright guard the accessible markup on every release.
sections.imageAlt: 501 Feature Cards documentation and configuration section

decisions.choice: A Web Component instead of a React package
decisions.why: One tag drops into any CMS or framework without shipping a framework runtime with it.
decisions.tradeoff: Theming must be exposed deliberately through custom properties and parts.

decisions.choice: Zod-validated configuration
decisions.why: Bad CMS input fails loudly in development rather than rendering a broken card in production.
decisions.tradeoff: The schema ships as part of the bundle.

decisions.choice: Vitest and Playwright against the published package
decisions.why: A component edited by non-developers must not regress silently.
decisions.tradeoff: A slower release loop than a small library would otherwise need.

caseStudy.outcome: Published as an installable npm Web Component with a live editor demo at 501fun.humza-butt.space, replacing hard-coded stat cards with accessible, CMS-editable ones.

projects.name: Monzo 1p Challenge Calculator
projects.description: Savings calculator inspired by the Monzo 1p challenge with 3 modes (Next N days, Month, Custom range), magic link auth, and PWA support

caseStudy.claim: Savings calculator inspired by the Monzo 1p challenge with 3 modes (Next N days, Month, Custom range), magic link auth, and PWA support
caseStudy.role: Sole engineer — calculator, accounts, and deploy
caseStudy.timeline: Shipped 2023 · rebuilt on Next.js and Cloudflare in 2026

metrics.label: calculation modes: next N days, month, custom range
total saved over a full 365-day challenge

caseStudy.problem:
The 1p challenge is simple arithmetic nobody wants to do by hand, and most online versions only compute the standard full year.

People join mid-year or want a specific window, so the calculator had to handle arbitrary ranges and remember the plan afterwards.

sections.title: Three calculation modes
sections.body:
Next N days, a calendar month, or a custom date range — each producing the daily schedule and running total.

Signed-in users keep their plan; everyone else can still run the numbers immediately.
sections.imageAlt: Monzo 1p challenge calculator with savings mode selection and totals

decisions.choice: Magic-link auth instead of passwords
decisions.why: Saving a plan should not require inventing and remembering another password.
decisions.tradeoff: Every sign-in depends on email delivery.

decisions.choice: Next.js on Cloudflare Workers via OpenNext
decisions.why: Server rendering and edge delivery without leaving the Workers platform.
decisions.tradeoff: An adapter sits between the framework and the runtime.

decisions.choice: PWA install
decisions.why: A savings tracker gets reopened from a phone home screen, not bookmarked.
decisions.tradeoff: Service-worker caching must never serve stale figures.

caseStudy.outcome: Live at monzo-1p-challenge-calculator.online with three calculation modes, magic-link accounts, saved plans, Vitest and Playwright coverage, and offline-capable PWA install.

projects.name: Brute-forcer
projects.description: Privacy-focused password entropy and crack-time estimator—client-side math, no real brute forcing, embedded live demo

caseStudy.claim: Privacy-focused password entropy and crack-time estimator—client-side math, no real brute forcing, embedded live demo
caseStudy.role: Sole engineer
caseStudy.timeline: Shipped 2023 · rebuilt on Next.js and Cloudflare in 2026

metrics.label: passwords sent to a server — all maths client-side

caseStudy.problem:
Password strength meters either ask you to type a real password into someone else’s server, or reduce strength to a vague colour bar.

The honest version has to run entirely in the browser and show the entropy behind the estimate.

sections.title: Entropy and crack-time estimates
sections.body:
Character-set and length analysis produce an entropy figure, which is turned into crack-time estimates across attacker profiles.

Everything runs in the page, and the live demo is embedded directly in the case study.
sections.imageAlt: Brute-forcer password entropy and crack-time estimation interface

decisions.choice: All calculation client-side
decisions.why: A password strength tool that transmits the password defeats its own purpose.
decisions.tradeoff: No server-side analytics on what people test.

decisions.choice: Estimate crack time rather than actually brute forcing
decisions.why: Entropy maths answers the question instantly; real cracking would be slow and prove nothing.
decisions.tradeoff: Results are model-based rather than empirical.

decisions.choice: Next.js on Workers via OpenNext
decisions.why: Static-fast delivery with room for server features later.
decisions.tradeoff: More build machinery than a plain static page needs.

caseStudy.outcome: Live at bruteforcer.online: client-side entropy and crack-time estimation with an embedded live demo, and no password ever leaving the browser.

projects.name: Gremlins
projects.description: Playful Windows tray companion—configurable gremlins, quiet hours, panic mode, and a local-first marketing site.

caseStudy.claim: Playful Windows tray companion—configurable gremlins, quiet hours, panic mode, and a local-first marketing site.
caseStudy.role: Sole engineer — WPF tray app and marketing site
caseStudy.timeline: Shipped 2023 · Microsoft Store release maintained through 2026

metrics.label: data leaving the machine — local-first by design
panic key to stop everything instantly

caseStudy.problem:
Desktop prank apps are all-or-nothing: funny for a minute, then genuinely disruptive during a meeting or a screen share.

Gremlins needed a mischief engine with real guardrails — scheduling, quiet hours, safety profiles, and an instant off switch.

sections.title: Configurable gremlins
sections.body:
Each gremlin is an individually toggled behaviour with its own settings, so users assemble the mischief they actually want.

A native WPF tray app keeps it out of the way until it fires.
sections.imageAlt: Gremlins app window listing configurable gremlin behaviours

sections.title: Rules, timing, and quiet hours
sections.body:
Frequency, timing windows, and quiet hours decide when anything is allowed to happen.

This is the difference between a joke and an app people uninstall after one meeting.
sections.imageAlt: Gremlins rules and timing configuration with quiet hours

sections.title: Safety profiles and panic mode
sections.body:
Safety profiles cap what gremlins may do, and panic mode stops everything immediately from the tray.

The rules engine behind both is covered by xUnit tests.
sections.imageAlt: Gremlins safety profile settings and panic mode controls

sections.title: Local-first marketing site
sections.body:
gremlins.site explains the app and links the Microsoft Store listing, built with React and Vite on Cloudflare Workers.

It matches the app’s local-first stance: nothing about your gremlins is reported back.
sections.imageAlt: Gremlins marketing site landing page at gremlins.site

decisions.choice: WPF and Win32 rather than Electron
decisions.why: A background companion has to be light on memory and native to Windows tray and notification behaviour.
decisions.tradeoff: Windows-only, with no code shared with the web surface.

decisions.choice: Quiet hours, safety profiles, and a panic key
decisions.why: The joke stops being funny during a screen share; users need an off switch they trust.
decisions.tradeoff: Far more configuration surface than a one-button prank.

decisions.choice: Local-first — settings and data stay on the device
decisions.why: A prank app that phones home is an instant no from users and from IT.
decisions.tradeoff: No telemetry to diagnose problems in the wild.

caseStudy.outcome: Shipped on the Microsoft Store with configurable gremlins, scheduling and quiet hours, safety profiles, panic mode, xUnit-tested rules, and a marketing site at gremlins.site.

projects.name: FireWatch - Fire Intelligence Dashboard
projects.description: Geospatial wildfire intelligence dashboard with map-based risk analysis and metre-accurate proximity checks for analysts.

caseStudy.claim: Geospatial wildfire intelligence dashboard with map-based risk analysis and metre-accurate proximity checks for analysts.
caseStudy.role: Full-stack engineer — Angular client, Express/PostGIS API, and Docker deploy
caseStudy.timeline: 2026 · source public on GitHub, no public deployment

metrics.label: metre-accurate proximity and containment queries

caseStudy.problem:
Wildfire analysts need to know what a fire is actually near — homes, roads, protected land — not just where the hotspot sits on a basemap.

Approximate distance maths over latitude and longitude breaks down at exactly the scale that matters, so proximity had to be computed with real geospatial types.

sections.title: Map-based risk analysis
sections.body:
An Angular and OpenLayers client for inspecting hotspots, toggling layers, and running proximity queries against analyst-supplied assets, backed by an Express API over PostGIS.

There is no public deployment to screenshot, so this case study leads with a product card rather than a live capture.
sections.imageAlt: FireWatch product card — geospatial wildfire intelligence dashboard for risk and proximity analysis

decisions.choice: PostGIS for spatial queries instead of app-side distance maths
decisions.why: Metre-accurate proximity and containment need real geography types and a spatial index.
decisions.tradeoff: A Postgres extension and spatial migrations become part of the deploy.

decisions.choice: OpenLayers over a hosted map SDK
decisions.why: Full control of layers and projections without per-tile vendor billing.
decisions.tradeoff: Considerably more map plumbing written by hand.

decisions.choice: Dockerised API and database
decisions.why: Geospatial stacks are painful to reproduce; the container pins the whole environment.
decisions.tradeoff: Heavier local setup than a serverless API would need.

caseStudy.outcome: A working analyst dashboard — Angular and OpenLayers client, Express API, PostGIS proximity queries — running from Docker with the source public on GitHub.

projects.name: Recount
projects.description: Productivity suite: Chrome MV3 extension tracks time by domain; Next.js app for marketing, dashboard, and admin; REST API on Express and Cloudflare (Hono) with Supabase, Stripe, and AI reports

caseStudy.claim: Productivity suite: Chrome MV3 extension tracks time by domain; Next.js app for marketing, dashboard, and admin; REST API on Express and Cloudflare (Hono) with Supabase, Stripe, and AI reports
caseStudy.role: Sole engineer — extension, web app, and API
caseStudy.timeline: Shipped 2023 · Cloudflare API and AI reporting added 2026

metrics.label: surfaces: MV3 extension, Next.js app, REST API
timers to start or stop — capture is passive

caseStudy.problem:
Time-tracking tools ask you to start and stop timers, so the data is only ever as honest as your memory.

Recount captures time by domain automatically in the browser, which then leaves the harder problem: turning a raw domain log into something worth reading.

sections.title: Marketing site, dashboard, and reports
sections.body:
A Chrome MV3 extension records time per domain and syncs to a Next.js dashboard with Recharts breakdowns and an admin surface.

OpenAI turns the raw log into a written activity report, with Stripe handling subscriptions and Resend the transactional mail.
sections.imageAlt: Recount marketing site introducing browser time tracking by domain

decisions.choice: A Chrome MV3 extension for passive capture
decisions.why: Automatic per-domain timing is more accurate than any manual timer.
decisions.tradeoff: The MV3 service-worker lifecycle makes long-running background timing fiddly.

decisions.choice: An Express API alongside a Hono Worker
decisions.why: Kept the existing Node API while moving latency-sensitive routes to the edge.
decisions.tradeoff: Two runtimes to deploy and keep behaviourally identical.

decisions.choice: AI summaries rather than charts alone
decisions.why: A short weekly narrative gets read; a bar chart of domains usually does not.
decisions.tradeoff: Per-report model cost and prompt maintenance.

caseStudy.outcome: Live at recount.world: an MV3 extension capturing time by domain, a Next.js dashboard and admin, a Supabase-backed API on Express and Hono, Stripe billing, and AI-written activity reports.

projects.name: Imposter
projects.description: Real-time multiplayer word imposter party game: Discord Activity (voice-channel embedded) and standalone web/PWA, one React client and authoritative PartyKit server

caseStudy.claim: Server-authoritative PartyKit multiplayer word-imposter game with Discord Activity support.
caseStudy.role: Sole engineer — React client, PartyKit server, and Discord Activity integration
caseStudy.timeline: Shipped 2023 · Discord Activity and PWA surfaces added 2026

metrics.label: surfaces from one client: Discord Activity and web/PWA
authoritative PartyKit server owning every room

caseStudy.problem:
A word imposter game only works if nobody can peek, so the secret word and role assignment cannot live in the client.

It also had to run where people already talk — inside a Discord voice channel — without maintaining a second codebase for the web version.

sections.title: One client, two surfaces
sections.body:
The same React client runs standalone as an installable PWA and embedded in a Discord voice channel through the Embedded App SDK.

Only the auth and context shim differs between them.
sections.imageAlt: Imposter game lobby with room join options in the web client

sections.title: Server-authoritative rounds
sections.body:
PartyKit holds room state over WebSockets: role assignment, the secret word, turn order, and voting all resolve on the server.

Supabase persists results, and i18next keeps the game playable beyond English.
sections.imageAlt: Imposter web client showing game setup options further down the page

decisions.choice: Server-authoritative PartyKit rooms
decisions.why: The imposter’s role and the secret word must never be inferable from the client bundle or the network tab.
decisions.tradeoff: Every state change is a round trip; the client cannot resolve rounds optimistically.

decisions.choice: One React client for Discord and the web
decisions.why: Discord’s Embedded App SDK renders a normal web app, so both surfaces share everything but the auth shim.
decisions.tradeoff: Discord’s iframe sandbox and CSP constrain what the web build can assume.

decisions.choice: i18next from the start
decisions.why: Party games spread by word of mouth, which crosses languages quickly.
decisions.tradeoff: Every copy change becomes a translation change.

caseStudy.outcome: Playable at imposter-game.site and as a Discord Activity inside voice channels, with server-authoritative rounds on PartyKit, Supabase persistence, PWA install, and Playwright coverage.

projects.name: Breathapplyser
projects.description: Modern breathalyzer app with advanced tracking, caffeine monitoring, social features, and comprehensive analytics (2026). Includes legacy version (2024).

caseStudy.claim: Breathalyzer companion with tracking, caffeine monitoring, and social features — owned backend end-to-end.
caseStudy.role: Founder and sole developer — Flutter app, Node API, and web surfaces

metrics.label: languages supported in-app
app stores shipped to (Google Play, App Store)

decisions.why: The right cost for an occasional-use utility with no revenue.
decisions.tradeoff: Cold starts, and the instance can be unavailable between uses.

caseStudy.outcome: A working browser-based PNG-to-vector converter deployed at pngtosvg-ulmg.onrender.com, kept as a small utility rather than a maintained product.

projects.name: Doppelgan-Car
projects.description: AI-powered car personality matcher

caseStudy.claim: AI car matcher that reasons over a personality questionnaire instead of scoring a fixed quiz lookup table.
caseStudy.role: Sole developer
caseStudy.problem:
"What car suits me?" is normally answered by a magazine quiz with a hard-coded lookup table behind it.

Doppelgan-Car runs a model over the answers so the match reasons about traits rather than counting quiz points.

sections.title: Personality questionnaire and match
sections.body:
A Nuxt front end collects the questionnaire and a Flask service runs the matching against OpenAI.

The result is an explained pairing rather than a bare car name.
sections.imageAlt: Doppelgan-Car landing page for the AI car personality matcher

decisions.choice: Model-based matching over a lookup table
decisions.why: Nuanced and free-text answers cannot be scored by a fixed rubric.
decisions.tradeoff: Results vary between runs and need guard-railing.

decisions.choice: Nuxt front end with a Flask API
decisions.why: Server-rendered questionnaire UI with the model work kept in Python.
decisions.tradeoff: Two hosting targets for a small project.

decisions.choice: Kept hidden on the portfolio
decisions.why: It is a novelty project that does not represent current work.
decisions.tradeoff: None — the deployment stays live for anyone with the link.

caseStudy.outcome: Live at doppelgang-car.vercel.app: a personality questionnaire that returns an AI-reasoned car match, retained as an archived novelty project.

projects.name: Tindev
projects.description: Developer-focused networking platform for tech professionals

caseStudy.claim: Developer networking prototype pairing profile-based matching with peer-to-peer WebRTC video introductions.
caseStudy.role: Sole developer
caseStudy.problem:
Developer networking happens in crowded chat servers where introductions rarely turn into an actual conversation.

Tindev paired profile matching with a direct video call, so a match could become a conversation in one step instead of a dead DM.

sections.title: Profile matching and video calls
sections.body:
Firebase-backed profiles drive matching and double as the WebRTC signalling channel for peer-to-peer video.

The prototype was never publicly deployed, so this case study uses a product card rather than a live capture.
sections.imageAlt: Tindev product card — developer networking prototype with matching and WebRTC video

decisions.choice: Peer-to-peer WebRTC video
decisions.why: Direct calls avoid relaying media through a server we would have to pay for and secure.
decisions.tradeoff: NAT traversal and signalling still need infrastructure.

decisions.choice: Firebase for profiles, matching, and signalling
decisions.why: Realtime documents double as a WebRTC signalling channel with no extra service.
decisions.tradeoff: Matching and call setup are both tied to one vendor.

decisions.choice: Left as a prototype
decisions.why: A matching pool is a distribution problem, not an engineering one, and the distribution was not there.
decisions.tradeoff: Working code with no users.

caseStudy.outcome: A functional prototype — profile matching plus WebRTC video introductions — shelved before public launch and kept hidden on the portfolio.
